deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page: no formulas, derivations or computations. The page continues Riemann's 'Excerpte aus Lamé' begun on the previous folio. It is a verbatim copy, in French, of a passage from G. Lamé, 'Leçons sur la théorie mathématique de l'élasticité des corps solides' (Paris 1852), p. 332, Leçon XXIV, §134. This is the concluding lesson, in which Lamé reflects on method.

Content of the passage:
(i) All questions of molecular physics have been held back, not advanced, by extending the principles of celestial mechanics too early, if not wrongly.
(ii) The geometers (Laplace, Poisson, Navier and others are implied) were used to explaining all celestial phenomena by universal gravitation. They came to believe that attraction, that is ponderable matter alone, must also explain most terrestrial phenomena. They took it as the starting point for capillarity theory and for elasticity theory.
(iii) Progress in general physics will probably lead one day to a principle analogous to universal gravitation, of which gravitation would be only a corollary. That principle would ground a rational theory covering both celestial and terrestrial mechanics.
(iv) To presuppose this principle, or to infer it entirely from one of its parts, was to delay its discovery, perhaps for a long time.

Relation to the rest of the excerpt: this continues the theme of the excerpts on the previous page, from pp. 11 and 37–38. There Lamé argues that the elasticity equations should be obtained without hypothetical central attraction/repulsion laws. He holds that force laws should come out as consequences, as universal gravitation did from Kepler's laws. He also criticizes Navier's and Poisson's 'intégration autour d'un point' for assuming continuous matter.

Why Riemann copied it (interpretive): the selection fits his own natural-philosophy programme in the Naturphil fragments. That programme seeks a unified, field/ether-mediated (contact-action) principle, from which gravitation and the other forces follow, in place of Newtonian action at a distance. This is a reading-note page only; nothing is derived.

results.what: Verbatim excerpt of Lamé's methodological critique: the extension of Newtonian attraction (celestial mechanics) to molecular physics was premature, and a more general unifying principle should be sought, of which gravitation would be a corollary.
results.modern_name: Critique of the Laplace–Poisson molecular (central-force) programme in elasticity/capillarity; call for a unified field-type principle
results.usually_credited_to: Gabriel Lamé, Leçons sur la théorie mathématique de l'élasticité des corps solides (1852), §134

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a reading excerpt copied from Lamé's published 1852 textbook, with no mathematics and no original commentary. That Riemann read Lamé, and was sympathetic to anti-action-at-a-distance views, fits his known natural-philosophy fragments. It is a minor biographical/source detail only.
transcription_corrections: Page reference: the image reads 'p. 332.' (Lamé's book ends around p. 335 and Leçon XXIV is its last lesson), not 'p. 532.'

'les deux Mécanique' — the manuscript appears to have a correction/overwriting at the start of the line ('les' written over another word). Lamé's printed text has 'les deux Mécaniques'; Riemann's copy seems to omit the plural -s.
'présupposer ce principe connu' — in the manuscript 'principe' and 'connu' are run together ('principeconnu'); the reading is otherwise correct.
